passages.title: Solution for: Children’s literature studies today
content: Who studies children's literature and what is it that they study? The answers to this question are complex and messy because of the many confounding factors that exist in this field.

Firstly, unlike literature for adults, children's literature is not generally written by its own readers. Adults write for children, and thus adult perceptions of what children are, and of what they could and should be, become woven into the literature.

Furthermore, some of those who study children's literature (and those who write certain kinds of children's books) are less interested in literary values than in the kinds of lessons it can teach—either in terms of creating better children or in terms of serving a particular curriculum. The issue of how a teacher can use a children's book is often contentious, but even outside the classroom, much material for children is still didactic.

Thirdly, while almost all literature is currently promoted within a strong commercial matrix, children's literature is often especially targeted for marketing initiatives. This fact means that readers are often recruited with a message that is negligibly literary and significantly oriented to ideas of consumption. Daniel Hade (2002) has raised useful questions about whether children's experience of reading is altered when their books are part of a larger marketing framework involving the movie, the game, and the toy of a popular children's book. How children perceive and respond to their stories in this new context is an important question.

It is also important to note that texts in an ever-increasing range of new media compete with print media for the attention of the child reader and create definitional issues for scholars. Does the term literature exclusively imply a verbal text? If not, where are the limits? Could a literary computer game ever be considered a work of literature? If not, what kind of attention should be paid to it, since children themselves undoubtedly perceive their print literature as part of a broader continuum? The internet provides one forum through which children now communicate with each other. (In 2003, the internet search engine Google listed 7,920,000 sites relating to the Harry Potter novels; even allowing for duplication and dead ends, that is a number with revolutionary implications.)

Finally, in the context of the higher education institutions where the formal study of children's literature is often located, at least three disciplinary frameworks (English, education, and librarianship) fragment the focus of scholarly study of children's literature. How is the value of the imaginative encounter with the work of literature sustained and honoured among such a welter of conflicting interests? One route through this maze is to ask the child readers for help. As David Lewis (2001) has perceptively noted, what children think of reading is not usually the same as what adults think, whether teachers or parents. As Lewis points out, children "sometimes see more and they often see differently". If those who study reading can explore children's perceptions as well as those of adults, their understanding of the nature of reading will be enhanced.

Lewis makes a further valid point when he adds that exploring children's perceptions is usually justified for educational reasons. It is true that a better understanding of how children read and how they learn to read is a prerequisite to improved approaches to teaching. However, it can also be argued, as Lewis rightly does, that when children's responses to literature are accessed and interpreted, they frequently lead to an understanding of how picture books appeal to children.

Young people's accounts of what and how they read also enable a more sophisticated description of many of the complex processes involved in reading. All descriptions of reading run the risk of solipsism: this is how I read, so this is what reading is for everyone. Asking other readers how they read, however, reduces that risk. For example, if I am a strong visualiser as I read, I may consider that visualisation is a key component of successful reading and I may judge books by their capacity to evoke a vivid visual response. Other readers, however, may help me to realise that not everyone reads with mental pictures. Some readers respond to the patterns of the words, "hearing" them inaudibly like a subliminal radio programme. Others respond to the patterns of feelings in the story, responding with an emotional connection. Talking to competent readers, of all ages, provides a better understanding of reading experiences.

Children's insights are even more important when it comes to understanding the significance of print literature as one aspect of literary culture. Too often adults assume that reading any book at all is a more worthwhile experience than playing a digital game of any kind. A humbler approach would include asking why the game appeals to the player. Many adults will probably never develop the automatic skills to process a game as readily as they can read a book. This does not indicate that a book is better, but that a particular set of skills is absent. Non-players must acknowledge that some fictional universes are thus closed to them, and a logical response would be to find someone who can guide them to the pleasures and challenges of the gaming world. Games need to be judged individually just as books do, and any evaluative framework needs to take this into account.

transcript: [01:29] Sally: Morning. Thanks for coming round. I'm Sally.
[01:32] Man: Morning. Um, so just before we get started, I'll just make a few notes. So, um, we're at 15 Hill Street?
[01:41] Sally: Yes, that's right.
[01:43] Man: OK, great. And then I need to write down your contact information. Just for the office, you know. So first, what's your surname please, Sally?
[01:52] Sally: It's Keyworth. I'll spell that. K-E-Y-W-O-R-T-H.
[02:00] Man: And your phone number, I've got that somewhere. Yes, 027 584 6613.
[02:10] Sally: That's right.
[02:11] Man: OK Sally, so what building work would you like to have done?

[02:15] Sally: Well, let's go into the kitchen first. So, you see, it's quite dark in here. We've tried having a few lights fitted, but it hasn't really made any difference. So what we've decided is the window is too small.
[02:30] Sally: We'd like a larger one.
[02:32] Man: That shouldn't be a problem. And is there anything else you'd like done in the kitchen?
[02:36] Sally: Well, at this time of year, I mean, I shouldn't complain really, but I wish it wasn't so hot in here. Is there anything you can do about that?
[02:46] Man: Air conditioning?
[02:47] Sally: It's too expensive.
[02:48] Man: How about a fan then?
[02:50] Sally: Yes, that would be perfect.
[02:52] Man: Right. And what's next, Sally?

[02:55] Sally: Well, if we walk through into the bathroom, the thing is, when my father's staying, he can't use the bath. So I thought here, on the back wall, I'd like you to fit a shower. Is that possible?
[03:08] Man: Shouldn't be too hard. I'll get you some brochures, because there are a few ways of doing that.
[03:13] Sally: Thanks.
[03:14] Man: Now, those tiles on the wall look new. So do you want to keep those?
[03:18] Sally: Yes, the tiles are new, but actually my husband doesn't like them. We want to change to those very small ones. But do I have to choose a colour now?
[03:28] Man: You can do that later. I'll get some charts for you to look at.
[04:15] Sally: Now the last thing, let's walk outside. I need to show you some things outside the house.
[04:23] Man: Right. Ooh, nice garden. And the fence looks in good condition.
[04:28] Sally: Yes, it's new, but the thing is the gate. It's too low. You have to bend down to open it. We need something that's higher.
[04:36] AUDIO: <v Right, I'll see to that.
[04:38] Sally: Then the other thing is the garage here. We had a break-in, actually.
[04:43] Man: Ah, yeah, I can see. Um, the door should be fine, but the lock. I'll replace that, shall I?
[04:51] Sally: Yes, thanks. Then also, if you step back here and look up on the roof, you can see that it's damaged.
[04:58] Man: Did that happen in the storm a couple of weeks ago?
[05:01] Sally: Yes, that's right.
[05:02] Man: I'll get up there and take a look at that then. That might be quite a big job, but I'll get back to you once I've had a look.
[05:08] Sally: OK.
[05:08] Man: I can see that your rain gutter is broken as well.
[05:11] Sally: Can you fix that?
[05:13] Man: Well, I'll need to replace it, maybe with a steel one. It'd be stronger.
[05:17] Sally: No, plastic will be fine, thanks. It's cheaper.
[05:22] Sally: And that's everything, I think. Is there any other information you need? What about a start date?
[05:28] Man: Well, I'm completely booked all April, and I've got a job on May the 5th. That'll be a few days. So, let's say May the 8th.
[05:39] Sally: OK.
[05:39] Man: Now, what about a key, in case you're out?
[05:42] Sally: We have a security code. I'll give you that. It's a mix of letters and numbers. The code is A-G-4-1-7-6.
[05:53] Man: Got that. OK, we'll organise some...

passages.title: The McFaddin hiking and nature trail
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "The McFaddin hiking and nature trail"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:52] AUDIO: Good morning. I'm Susan Meyer, trail warden for the McFadden Hiking and Nature Trail. Let me tell you a bit about the trail. The trail is 25 miles long, running roughly east to west.

[01:08] AUDIO: To hike it, you may start at either end of the trail or in between. You can hike the whole length of the trail, or just a couple of miles, because there are 20 entry points along the trail, each connected to public roads by short paths. For hikers coming from Johnson City, there's a shuttle bus to each of the two end points every morning and evening, and four of the entry points have a free car park with television camera surveillance. At one-mile intervals along the trail, there are rest stations providing picnic areas, water, toilets, and places where you can recharge your electronic devices.

[01:56] AUDIO: In response to a poll of walkers last year, we've recently installed kiosks at each rest station with clear, easy-to-follow maps and other trail information. There are several distinct sections of trail. The Red Rock Walk offers a superb opportunity to study a huge variety of vegetation along the way. There's lots to look at, though you can't see great distances.

[02:26] AUDIO: Birds are actually hard to spot, but with a pair of binoculars and at certain times of day, you may see some rare varieties. The River Walk comprises about five miles of trail winding along the bank of the Mulder River. Personally, I prefer this section of the trail in winter. The river does freeze over and the snow can accumulate, but that doesn't always discourage visitors.

[02:59] AUDIO: Sometimes, though, if the weather conditions are really unsuitable, we might have to close this walk to the public. But often it can get crowded with hikers who've discovered the attraction of the area. Now let me tell you about the Halfway Hostel, located approximately midway along the trail. It has a range of facilities available to help make your walking experience memorable.

[04:12] AUDIO: Let me give you some information about the various facilities available there. Of course, there are beds in dormitories for use at a very reasonable $7 per person, weekdays or weekends. Unfortunately, we found that pre-booking beds just didn't work, so now we allocate them as people arrive, but we have extra cots and sleeping bags to help with any overflow. There are two family rooms accommodating six people each with private bathrooms.

[04:46] AUDIO: They're $35 per room, and for them you will need to make arrangements ahead of time as they're very popular, especially at the weekends. A popular facility that we've recently added is coin-operated washing machines for your clothes. You can get awfully wet and dirty if you're walking the trail in bad weather, and since we got these machines, you can put on clean gear when you set out in the morning. The hostel serves two meals a day, breakfast at $4 and dinner at $8.

[05:23] AUDIO: The same for adults and kids. There's always a vegetarian and a non-vegetarian option, depending on your preferences. We do ask you to give a hand with serving and cleaning up after meals. We have plenty of showers and unlimited hot water available, so you can have this luxury at no charge, and you can enjoy it as long as you like.

[05:49] AUDIO: Now, some people like to spend time on the trail on mountain bikes and maybe take a bit of a rest from all that walking, and that's permitted as long as you observe basic safety rules. The hostel's in the process of creating a bike rental scheme, which should be up and running next year. So, if you think...

Cụm “recently added” cho thấy đây là tiện ích mới được bổ sung gần đây . Trong các lựa chọn, ý này khớp với new equipment → chọn G . 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ E => Dễ nhầm vì nhiều tiện ích ở hostel là miễn phí , nhưng máy giặt được nói rõ là coin-operated nên không free . ❌ C => Dễ chọn nếu

passages.title: A marketing project on food packaging
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "A marketing project on food packaging"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:59] Tutor: Hello Pam, Jason. Thanks for coming to discuss your marketing project. I've read your proposal and outline, so let's go over it.
[01:08] Pam: Okay.
[01:08] Jason: Right.
[01:09] Tutor: You've chosen the topic of food packaging. So what did you want to get out of doing this project?
[01:16] Jason: We decided if we did our project on packaging, we might find some practical tips on how a business could make more money.
[01:23] Pam: After all, we're business admin students and that's the ultimate reason we're on the course, isn't it? So although we know the impact of packaging on the environment is important...
[01:33] Jason: We feel the government regulations are pretty strict already in that area.
[01:37] Tutor: Okay. Now you've decided to look specifically at the packaging of food, what do you think the main issue is for shoppers these days?

[01:46] Pam: Some people get upset about the waste with all the plastic and stuff used to package food, but I guess most don't pay much attention to that. A few years ago, people seemed concerned about packaging food so that buyers knew more about what it contains from labels, like calories, additives, and stuff.
[02:06] Jason: But in the current economic climate, Pam and I think people are most interested in packaging that helps keep food fresh for longer.
[02:14] Tutor: And you've chosen to concentrate on big supermarket chains. Why not look at local stores or even convenience stores?

[02:21] Jason: Well, there are some interesting published studies based on small retail outlets and we looked at those, but after a little investigation, we found that the managers of the large supermarkets in this area wanted to be helpful and are willing to let us talk to them and their employees.
[02:40] Pam: Of course, the supermarkets do account for most food sales around here, but that wasn't our reason for choosing them.

[02:48] Tutor: Speaking of this area, you know the food buying choices here are quite unusual. Since we're in a university town, the population is quite young, but actually my research shows that age isn't the factor in making the area unique. And although the education level is pretty high, that doesn't seem very important either.
[03:08] Jason: I guess it's because we got people from all over the world living here, with all the foreign students at university.
[03:15] Tutor: That's it. Our supermarkets cater for a huge diversity of cultures.

[03:20] Pam: In our survey of the literature, I was struck by what shoppers say is most important to them when they buy. I would have thought how much the buyer had to pay would be the key, but that doesn't appear to be the case.
[03:34] Jason: That's right. How delicious the buyer considers the product seems to be the main thing. Whether or not the food is good for you is pretty low down on the customer's priorities.

[03:44] Tutor: That's interesting. Let's discuss the practical experiment you're planning. You're going to design the box for a new breakfast cereal which you'll try to market. Not in reality, of course, but by showing different designs to some of your fellow students on a computer, a kind of virtual reality supermarket, and the students will choose the design that appeals most.
[04:49] Tutor: Let's talk through the experiment, okay?
[04:51] Jason: That'd be helpful.

[04:53] Tutor: Now, the number of different designs you're proposing to show each student is two. If I were you, I'd make it at least four. That way you can examine their reaction to more variety in the kinds of packaging.
[05:06] Pam: Okay, good idea. We do have several more designs. Now, we've got a sample from our class of about 20. Is that enough?
[05:16] Tutor: Probably not. Try talking to the assistant in the business studies department. He can sort out how to recruit some more from other classes for you.
[05:25] Jason: Right.

[05:26] Tutor: Now, as to how you're going to display your packages to the students, I did talk about those technical issues in one of your first classes. Go back and look over what I said about the practical realities of conducting experiments.
[05:40] Jason: Okay, we can do that.
[05:42] Pam: We're going to ask each student to choose the one design they think is best, but how will we know why they chose that one?
[05:51] Tutor: Well, don't just rely on oral prompts. Give them a series of written questions. That way you'll have hard data.
[05:58] Jason: Okay.
[05:59] Tutor: But what about analyzing the data?
[06:02] Jason: Well, we've got an excellent computer program to gather it all together, but we still need to interpret it ourselves.
[06:09] Pam: So, we'll need to give ourselves a few more days for that.
[06:13] Jason: Yes, we will.
[06:14] Tutor: Anyway, it's all looking good.

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "We're going to ask each student to choose the one design they think is best, but how will we know why they chose that one? Well, don't just rely on oral prompts. Give them a series of written questions. That way you'll have hard data. Okay."
explanation.step3: 📌 Tìm vị trí : finding the reasons for students' choices ✅ Đáp án đúng : F ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Ngay sau câu “We're going to ask each student to choose the one design they think is best, but how will we know why they chose that one?” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Cụm cần nghe là “how will we know why they chose that one” → đây chính là ý hỏi về lý do sinh viên chọn thiết kế . Ngay sau đó, tutor trả lời: “don’t just rely on oral prompts” → nghĩa là không nên chỉ hỏi miệng . Tutor tiếp tục nói: “Give them a series of written questions.” → written questions tương ứng với việc thiết kế một bảng câu hỏi / questionnaire . Vì vậy, cách để tìm ra lý do lựa chọn của sinh viên là design a questionnaire → chọn F . 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ G => Dễ nhầm vì Pam đang nói về
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: design a questionnaire

questions.prompt: Match the statement/item with the correct option: "analysis of data collected"

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "But what about analyzing the data? Well, we've got an excellent computer program to gather it all together, but we still need to interpret it ourselves. So, we'll need to give ourselves a few more days for that. Yes, we will."
explanation.step3: 📌 Tìm vị trí : analysis of data collected ✅ Đáp án đúng : D ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Ngay sau câu “But what about analyzing the data?” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Từ khóa của câu hỏi là analysis of data collected nên cần nghe đoạn nói về việc xử lý / phân tích dữ liệu sau khi thu thập . Ngay sau câu hỏi của tutor: “But what about analyzing the data?” , Jason nói họ có computer program để gather it all together . Tuy nhiên, Jason nói tiếp: “we still need to interpret it ourselves” → nghĩa là phần phân tích / diễn giải dữ liệu vẫn cần tự làm, không xong ngay được. Pam sau đó kết luận: “So, we’ll need to give ourselves a few more days for that.” Cụm “give ourselves a few more days” tương đương với allow for more time → chọn D . 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ E => Dễ nhầ
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: allow for more time

passages.title: Science in the Future
content: 📌 Science in the Future
Science were asked to predict changes in their own field in the next 50 years

Computer science
The invention of computers is as significant as the discovery of how to create and use [ _____ ].
Computers will be seen as being [ _____ ].

Psychology
Research will become much more [ _____ ], and also more practical since more [ _____ ] will be working in the field.
Imaging devices will give information about the behaviour of the  [ _____ ].

Genetics
With increased life expectancy, it is important to consider the [ _____ ] of elderly people’s lives.
Knowledge of a person’s genome will indicate whether they are likely to be affected by a [ _____ ].
The approach to treatment will be on an increasingly [ _____ ] basis.

Zoology
People can explore the world via satellite.
For example, it is possible to see the effects of the destruction of [ _____ ] in East Africa.
Such increased awareness should enable us to do more to look after the [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:02] AUDIO: In this final lecture of our course on the history of science, I would like to look to the future and tell you about some predictions that have been made about scientific developments. The content for my talk is based on some research in which 30 scientific leaders were invited to comment on the developments that they envisage as likely to come about in their own discipline within 50 years. After summarizing some of their most interesting contributions for you, I'll ask you to give me your opinions as to the likelihood of these changes occurring within this timescale. You may also like to suggest some other likely changes yourselves.

[00:47] AUDIO: So first, let's start with computer science, as this is clearly an area where there are bound to be dramatic developments, and even more significantly, perhaps, these developments are likely to impact on every other field of learning. The invention of computers represents an enormous leap forward in the field of human endeavor. It could indeed be considered as being as momentous a development as when our predecessors in caves first learned to make fire and use it for all sorts of purposes. In the future, the computational revolution is certain to be generally recognized as a transformation as significant as, say, the industrial revolution.

[01:37] AUDIO: The computer scientists in the study I referred to felt that, in the coming decades, lives will be significantly enhanced by automated reasoning systems of different types. There was considerable agreement that people will increasingly perceive these computer systems as intelligent. Although many of these will be deployed behind the scenes, others will be in the foreground, serving in an elegant, often collaborative manner, to help people do their jobs, to learn and teach, to reflect and remember, to plan and decide. Without going into further detail about this at this point, let's turn to what predictions psychologists had to make.

[02:25] AUDIO: Their key point was that psychological research would inevitably become increasingly varied. It would move into such areas as behavioral economics and social neuroscience. There is likely to be further expansion into domains with more practical relevance as increasing numbers of women become research scientists, so areas such as health, environment, family and social identity will receive more attention. At the same time as they broaden their horizons, psychologists will also intensify their search to discover what exactly determines how we act.

[03:08] AUDIO: They will be assisted in this by imaging devices that will be inserted into the brain and provide a great deal of information about how it behaves. There should be some fascinating discoveries coming to light very soon. Another field that is currently undergoing enormous changes is that of genetics. It is not new to suggest that average life expectancy is likely to continue rising in most countries.

[03:40] AUDIO: However, today geneticists emphasize that it is vital that the increasing number of the elderly in society must take quality of life into account. So how will genetics help this to happen? To start with, they hope to develop technologies that can sequence each person's genome extremely cheaply. This information about our DNA enables health care providers to predict our likelihood of suffering from any particular disease.

[04:14] AUDIO: From there on, it is a matter of weighing up various factors with a view to determining what can be done to minimize each individual's level of risk. With such information in hand, new treatments will be developed, and the current one-size-fits-all approach to health care will give way to a more personal approach. The final subject area that I wish to bring to your attention is that of zoology. Once again, computers and technology have a key role to play here.

[04:50] AUDIO: Experts comment specifically on the importance of satellites for future developments in this field. These enable people to explore the world from their homes, offices, and schools. It is now possible, for instance, to go online and see for yourself the abundant wildlife in one part of East Africa and in the surrounding region the harm people have done by destroying the forests, all supposedly in the name of development. Zoologists believe the breakthrough that lies ahead is how people act on such information as this.

[05:30] AUDIO: They hope that we will learn to connect our minds to our hearts and apply this knowledge to help protect our planet. They express a clear hope that a greater understanding of the consequences of human short-sightedness will make people anxious to rectify what we can before it is too late.

passages.title: Winsham Farm Education Centre
content:
Address: Winsham Farm
[ _____ ] Road
Near Sherbone
Postcode:[ _____ ]
transcript: [02:31] Woman: Hello, Wynsham Farm Centre.
[02:34] Man: Oh, hello. I want to arrange a weekend away for myself and some people from work and we heard about your centre. I wonder if you could give me some details.
[02:44] Woman: Yes, certainly. We are a residential centre attached to a working farm and we organize educational activities for those guests who want them. What else would you like to know?
[02:58] Man: Well, firstly, what kind of accommodation have you got?
[03:02] Woman: We've got eight rooms altogether and we can sleep 38 at any one time. Three of the rooms have got six bunks and five of them have got four bunks.
[03:13] Man: Right, and what other facilities are there?

[03:16] Woman: We have separate toilets and showers for each of the rooms. There's a large dining room and a large meeting room which can be booked by groups in advance but I'm afraid we had a flood in there last month and the floor was slightly damaged so unfortunately it's out of use just now. We've got workmen coming in next week. When were you thinking of staying?
[03:40] Man: In three weeks time, the 28th of September.
[03:43] Woman: Oh, it should be okay by then.
[03:45] Man: Oh well, that's okay then. And what about food? Do you provide meals or is it self-catering?

[03:52] Woman: We're very flexible. As long as you give us enough notice we can cater for you or if you prefer you can just bring your own food and use the kitchen facilities. And some people prefer to eat out which is also fine.
[04:07] Man: Fine, and I heard that your farm is organic. Does that mean that you only have crops and no animals?

[04:14] Woman: It doesn't actually. A lot of people seem to think that but we do rear livestock as well and so we have a wide range of food. Organic means it's all produced without the use of artificial fertilisers or pesticides.
[04:30] Man: I see, that sounds good. Could you tell me what sort of recreational activities are available either at the centre or in the area?

[04:39] Woman: Yes, here at the centre we offer farm tours. They're very popular. One of the farm managers shows people around and explains some of the principles of organic farming and for any visitors who are really keen he'll let them drive a tractor or feed the animals and so on, with supervision of course.
[05:00] Man: I think a lot of our group would be interested in that. It'd make a change from factory work.
[05:05] Woman: Well, if they fancy it, tell them to come prepared. Plenty of old clothing, especially footwear. It can be very messy and wet.
[05:14] Man: OK, I'll warn them.

[06:04] Woman: And another type of activity we do is survival courses, but that's only for groups of five or more, and they've got to be acquaintances. They have to cooperate closely. These courses are very popular, especially with school groups, but adults seem to enjoy them too.
[06:22] Man: What do they involve? Things like map reading?

[06:25] Woman: Well, not exactly. What it is, we've got a large area of woodland on the farm and we run this course there. It's mainly about collecting food and water, lighting a fire without any equipment, that kind of thing.
[06:42] Man: This weekend could be hard work. What about the area around the centre? What is there to do?

[06:49] Woman: If you look at a map, you'll see that we're very well situated here. Our centre's about midway between the Exmoor National Park, which is very popular for hill walking, and the South Coast, which has very good beaches.
[07:03] Man: Are they both within walking distance?

[07:05] Woman: Well, they're both a bit far, unless you're very fit, but they're only about 30 minutes by road. And there's also a cycle path which starts quite near here, about 10 minutes walk away. You can hire bikes at the starting point.
[07:20] Man: What is there to do if the weather's bad? I hope it won't be, but you never know.

[07:24] Woman: Yes, that's right. Well, on most Saturday evenings we show films here, and then once a month a group of local musicians performs in our meeting room. And then Sherbourne is only 14 miles away. It's only a small town, but it's got a very good museum and an old abbey, which is well worth a visit.
[07:45] Man: Well, it sounds perfect for our purposes. One last thing. What about prices? I'm not sure yet, but there'll probably be about 15 of us.

[07:55] Woman: We charge a standard £14 a head for accommodation, whether there are 10 or 20 of you or whatever, and about £7 for cooked meals, depending on the menu you want. Use of the kitchen facilities is extra, as is the hire of the meeting room. It depends really what exactly you want and for how many people.
[08:18] Man: Right. Well, I've made a note of all that and I'll discuss it with the rest of the group. Then I'll get back to you with a firm booking. Can I do that by phone?
[08:27] Woman: Yes, you can. But once you've made a booking, we would need a deposit within five days to secure it. Then you just pay the balance when you're here.
[08:35] Man: Oh, yes, of course. Could you give me the address, please?
[08:40] Woman: Yes, it's Wynsham Farm, Cotehele Road, that's C-O-T-E-H-E-L-E, near Sherbourne. And the postcode is S-H-12-1-L-Q.
[09:00] Man: Thank you.

passages.title: Students’ Experiences with Vacation Jobs
content: Vacation jobMain advantageMain disadvantageRecommendationStocktaking[ _____ ]tiring[ _____ ]Office workair conditioning[ _____ ]choose a [ _____ ]Theme park attendant[ _____ ]rude customers[ _____ ]
transcript: [00:46] AUDIO: Welcome to Student Life. It's spring, and many of you may be thinking about arranging work for the long vacation. So on today's programme, Roger Anwell reports on a survey we conducted into the pleasures and problems of vacation jobs. Roger.

[01:03] AUDIO: Thank you, Sarah. Well, the first thing to say is that by far the majority of students we surveyed did just three types of jobs. All of these obviously had their advantages and disadvantages. Starting with stocktaking in supermarkets, the thing that students said they enjoyed most about this job was the travelling.

[01:23] AUDIO: They were often required to go to branches to do their stocktakes, and this was regarded as an interesting plus. The main negative, however, was that they tended to find the job tiring, with long hours spent on their feet and climbing high shelves. Now, one thing we did ask the students in our survey was whether they had any recommendations for other people taking on their job, and they said, perhaps not surprisingly, get good shoes. That's the only way you can keep going.

[01:51] AUDIO: Another job which lots of students did was office work, and the positive feature of this actually rather surprised me, until I remembered what a hot summer it was last year. Lots of students named air conditioning as the best thing about office work. The downside, which many talked about, was wearing formal clothes. Obviously this didn't go down too well with students.

[02:15] AUDIO: The advice most people gave was to select a large office. That way you have more variety of social contacts. Otherwise the work can get very boring. The third job which had attracted large numbers of students was as a theme park attendant, and again I got a surprise here because the big plus people talked about was good pay.

[02:38] AUDIO: It must have improved since my day, I must say. Anyway, the downside I did recognise, having to deal with difficult customers, especially in the heat when tempers get frayed. Not easy. And people said that it was a good idea to live nearby because there's a lot of shift work and you don't have to worry about transport at difficult times of the day.

[03:36] AUDIO: So, those were the findings from the survey on the most common student jobs. But not all student jobs have to be mundane and boring. One of the students who responded in our survey spoke at length about his amazing job as a zoo attendant. Peter Marshall had read about work opportunities on the zoo website and just went along with a friend to talk to someone in personnel.

[03:59] AUDIO: He was offered a job there and then, as easy as that. In previous years he'd done singularly unexciting shop work, so he was very pleased to be doing such original work. He ended up working for just under three months, which was actually slightly more than he'd anticipated and meant that he had to miss part of university term time. But he said it was well worth it because he thinks he's found his future career path as a result of this experience.

[04:27] AUDIO: He loved working on the educational side, in particular helping young kids understand about the animals in their natural environment. He said it was the most intriguing thing he'd ever done. He tells us though that with final exams coming up, he won't be able to do any paid work this coming vacation, so why don't you apply? If you're interested in getting further information about the findings of the survey...

passages.title: Planning a Study Syndicate for Geology Exam Revision
content: 📌 Reasons for having study Syndicates:
Teaching one another is a good way to learn.
It gives the opportunity to [ _____ ].
Shared reading means fuller notes.
You can do [ _____ ].
DateGeology TopicName of Presenter9th May[ _____ ]Bob[ _____ ]Glaciated areasAndy23rd MayRock informationHelen and John[ _____ ]VolcanoesJohn

- Presentation should last for: 30 to [ _____ ] minutes
(plan time for [ _____ ])
- Sources of information:
BibliographyLibrary books[ _____ ]
- For the presentations, use:
Overahead projectorWhiteboard[ _____ ]
transcript: [00:46] Andy: Right then, are we ready, Bob, Helen?
[00:49] Bob: Yeah.
[00:50] Andy: And is someone taking notes for John? He's at a tutorial, isn't he?
[00:53] Bob: Yeah, I'll let him know what we agree.
[00:55] Andy: Good. Okay, well, first thing is, has anyone apart from me actually been in a study syndicate before?
[01:03] Helen: What does it actually involve, Andy?
[01:05] Andy: Well, the idea is that it's a way for us, for students to study together without a teacher.
[01:11] Helen: Oh yeah, right.

[01:12] Andy: When I did it last time, I found it helpful because, well, as I said, there's no teacher, so it means we're teaching one another. And I found I really learnt a lot through having to teach it myself. It seemed a very good way to learn.
[01:26] Helen: And presumably it gives us the chance to share ideas as well.
[01:30] Bob: And you get fuller notes if you're all doing the reading.

[01:34] Andy: That's right. And as well as that, because of that, really, you can do, you know, much deeper research. So I thought we could try it to revise what we've done on the geology course. Because I know this is the one that most of us are worried about, the geology exam.
[01:49] Helen: Right, yes.
[01:52] Bob: So the idea is we all look at a different topic, a different topic from the geology course, and then give a presentation and talk about it?
[02:01] Andy: That's right. I've drawn up the framework of a table which might be useful. Here, I've made a copy.
[02:07] Helen: Oh, thanks.
[02:08] Andy: For the first topic, I thought we could maybe do mountain building. Is that alright?
[02:13] Bob: Yeah, sure. Actually, would you mind if I did that? I'm quite interested in it.
[02:17] Andy: Right.
[02:18] Helen: Right.
[02:19] Andy: So is May 9th OK for that?
[02:22] Bob: Yeah.
[02:22] Andy: I'll just write that down. And it's Bob for mountain building. And the following week, it can't be May 16th because of our tutorial. But what about the 17th?
[02:32] Helen: OK.
[02:33] Bob: And what about the next topic? What would be the next priority?
[02:38] Helen: Well, there's glaciated areas, but I don't want to do that.
[02:44] Bob: Fair enough.
[02:45] Andy: Actually, I don't mind having a bash. I did an assignment on them. Glaciated areas, Andy. Then we need someone to do rock formation.
[02:52] Andy: Helen?
[02:53] Helen: Yeah, OK. And John said he'd like to too, so you can put us both down for that.
[02:58] Andy: When?
[02:58] Helen: May 23rd would be best.
[03:01] Andy: Rock formation, Helen and John. Right. That really only leaves one week before the exams. Shall we make it on the 30th?
[03:08] Bob: I can't make it, I'm afraid.
[03:10] Andy: 29th of May? The exam's on June 3rd.
[03:14] Bob: Have to be.
[03:15] Andy: OK. Any ideas for a topic?
[03:18] Bob: John said he wouldn't mind doing something on volcanoes.
[03:22] Andy: Great. That's everyone then.
[04:02] Bob: And how long should these presentations be?
[04:05] Andy: Well, it's obviously up to us. In my experience, 30 minutes is about enough.
[04:10] Helen: Maybe a bit short. I'd have thought 40 minutes would be more like it.
[04:15] Andy: Well, shall we say 30 to 40 minutes? OK.
[04:18] Bob: And presumably time for questions?
[04:20] Helen: And discussion?
[04:21] Andy: Yes. Together they usually take about 20 minutes.
[04:25] Helen: Where shall we get the information from? Is it mainly lecture notes?
[04:29] Andy: Well, actually I suggest we avoid those because we already have all that information. I think it's better to go more deeply.
[04:35] Bob: We could use the bibliography.
[04:36] Andy: And anything else we find in the library, any other books.
[04:40] Helen: And articles, you know, from the journals.
[04:43] AUDIO: <v Bob. And then of course there's lots of stuff on the internet.
[04:46] Andy: Yes, that's the sort of thing.
[04:48] Bob: And what about the presentations? Will we just be talking? Presumably we can't use slides.
[04:54] Andy: It'd be a bit difficult, but we can use the OHP.
[04:57] Helen: And the whiteboard, of course.
[04:59] Bob: And we can make photocopies of our notes so everyone can have a copy.
[05:02] Andy: Yes, great. So is there anything else?

content: 📌 The Africa clawed frog (Xenopus laevis)

Description
∙ Skin is [ _____ ] and can vary in colour
∙ Skin is coated with a slippery film for [ _____ ]
∙ Males are [ _____ ] the size of females

Habitats
∙ Native to Africa
∙ Live in fresh water – preferred water that is [ _____ ]
∙ Can survive high levels of [ _____ ] in water
∙ Cannot survive if there is any metal in water
∙ In drought conditions, may live in [ _____ ] for up to a year

Diet
∙ Eat living or dead water creatures
∙ Find food using their sense of [ _____ ], their fingers, and their lateral lines
∙ Take food into their mouths using from legs and a [ _____ ] system

Other information
∙ Now popular as a pet in the US
∙ In some US states they are identified as a [ _____ ]
∙ Used in laboratories for developmental research
∙ Mucus from the skin was  [ _____ ] properties
transcript: [01:13] AUDIO: The aim of our study was to look at how naturally occurring substances can be used to treat infections, and we carried out a laboratory study using a frog called the African Clawed Frog, which has the scientific name Xenopus laevis. So, before I describe our study in detail, let me give you a general description about this frog. Like most other frogs, the African Clawed Frogs have a smooth skin. This is one way you can distinguish them from toads, whose skin is rough, and they can change the color of their skin to blend in with their surroundings.

[02:05] AUDIO: The surface of their skin also has another feature. It's covered with a layer of mucus. This makes it hard for other creatures to pick them up, and so it provides protection against predators. How big are they?

[02:23] AUDIO: Well, it depends on whether they're male or female, because the females, in this case, are a whole lot bigger than the males. A large-sized female may be 8 inches long, while the males are about half that size, so they're pretty small in comparison. What about their natural habitat? As their name suggests, these frogs are native to Africa, and they're found in most parts of Africa south of the Sahara Desert.

[03:00] AUDIO: They make their houses in fresh water, but they're rarely found in running streams. They like still water. As far as the temperature of the water goes, they're not too fussy. It can be warm or cool.

[03:17] AUDIO: They don't need to be in water where there are plants growing, and they can live in water that has quite a lot of salt in it. So they can live in brackish areas, such as marshes and estuaries. However, although they can live in a wide range of conditions, one thing that they are unable to tolerate is even very small traces of metal. That's immediately fatal to them.

[03:48] AUDIO: And that's important to remember when they're being kept in captivity. You've got to be careful what kind of tank you use and what you put into the water. In their natural habitat, the frogs normally live in water the whole time. But, in unfavorable conditions, such as drought, they can burrow into the mud and survive there for up to a year until conditions improve.

[04:23] AUDIO: As far as their diet is concerned, they're carnivorous. They eat other creatures they find in the water. And they're scavengers, which means they'll eat almost anything, living or dead. They've got huge appetites.

[04:44] AUDIO: Because the water they live in is often quite dirty and visibility is limited, they can't locate their food using their sense of sight. Instead, they use smell and also the sensitive fingers on their front legs. And they also have what's called a lateral line system on the sides of their bodies, which is sensitive to vibrations in the water. They use their front legs to get the food into their mouths, together with a type of pump arrangement that sucks the food into the mouth and down into their stomach.

[05:24] AUDIO: They don't have any teeth, so everything just goes straight down. Okay, well, although Xenopus started off in Africa, they're now quite widespread. One of the reasons for this is that a lot of people in the U.S. like keeping them at home as a pet. They're quite easy to look after and they can live for up to 20 years.

[05:54] AUDIO: But in some states of the U.S., such as California and Virginia, they have escaped from captivity and are reproducing in the wild and threatening native species there. So, they've been classified as a pest in these areas. But another very important use for the frogs is for research in laboratories. Because the females lay large numbers of eggs and the embryos are transparent, it's easy to see how they are developing, and so they're used for research into genetics and development, but also, the slippery mucus that covers their skin acts as an antibiotic, killing parasites and bacteria, and this is why we chose this frog for our research.
[06:51] AUDIO: So, let me describe the aim of our study.

passages.title: Places to visit with children
content: 📌 Places to visit with children

Alma Park
• Go to the zoo.
• A family ticket is $ [ _____ ].
• The fastest bus takes about [ _____ ] minutes.
• You can hold some animals and have a [ _____ ] for a small fee.

The Entertainment Room
• John [ _____ ] is performing.
• Performance run from Tuesday to [ _____ ].
• There is a [ _____ ] on tickets for Monday night’s preview.

The City
• Go to the city center [ _____ ] to see a special exhibition.
• Do origami – we’ll need to take a small [ _____ ].

Bunyabbie Island
• Explore with a four-wheel drive.
• Go snorkelling at Salty Lake – it’s on the [ _____ ] side of the Island.
• You’re not allowed to [ _____ ] on the island.
transcript: [01:39] Man: Good afternoon. Can I help you?

[01:42] Woman: Yes, I'm looking for some places to visit when my sister and her children come to stay. They arrive this weekend from overseas. I'm new to the area and don't really know what to recommend. Do you have any ideas?
[01:54] Man: What about going to Alma Park to visit the zoo?
[01:57] Woman: Oh, I like the idea of that. Is it reasonably priced?
[02:02] Man: Yes, it's not a bad price. A standard adult ticket is normally $30, but there's a special deal for families of $65, which is a saving of $35.
[02:12] Woman: That's a great deal. How do we get there from the city?
[02:16] Man: You can go by bus.
[02:17] Woman: Is it very far?

[02:19] Man: The 385 will get you there in approximately 40 minutes, depending on traffic. There is another bus, the 388, but it takes 20 minutes longer, so it's worth waiting a few more minutes for the more direct bus.
[02:32] Woman: OK. Are there any special things to do there? Can you feed the animals or anything like that?

[02:38] Man: They've stopped that, but most tourists love the fact that you're allowed to hold some of the animals and get your photo taken. They just ask you to make a small payment to help with costs.
[02:49] Woman: Oh, the kids would love that. My sister also likes going to the theatre. Is there anything good on at the moment? She especially likes comedies.

[02:58] Man: There's a place called the Entertainment Room in Ascot. I'll just check their website. Hmm, yes, there's a festival running at the moment with John Rosie as the main entertainer. He's really funny.
[03:11] Woman: How do you spell that? Is it R-O-Z-Y?
[03:14] Man: No, it's R-O-S-I-E.
[03:17] Woman: Got it. And when is it on?
[03:19] Man: Next week. It says it starts on Tuesday with a special matinee show on the Wednesday. It was supposed to finish on Friday, but because of the demand it's been extended to Saturday.
[03:31] Woman: It must be good then. Is it expensive?
[03:34] Man: I don't think so. Let's see. Oh, it says there's a special preview show on the Monday and they're offering a discount on tickets that night.
[03:43] Woman: We'll try and go then in that case. I also wanted to spend a day in the city centre. The children will get bored just looking at the shops. Is there anything else for them to do?
[04:29] Woman: What's the museum like?
[04:30] Man: It's very popular with children and there's a very hands-on exhibition on at the moment. They'd love that.
[04:37] Woman: Sounds good.
[04:37] Man: And there's a workshop on where they learn how to do origami.
[04:41] Woman: Will they need to bring anything special for that?

[04:44] Man: On this leaflet it says that things like scissors and all of the paper are provided. They just advise children to bring a box to carry the completed origami home in. Just a little one will do.
[04:56] Woman: I'm also looking for a weekend activity. I've heard Bunyabi Island is great. Would we need a car to get round the island?
[05:03] Man: A four-wheel drive is a great way to explore. You should also try snorkeling at Salty Lake.
[05:09] Woman: Is that in the centre of the island, near the mountain?
[05:12] Man: No, it's on the ocean side.

[05:14] Woman: OK, I'll get a map and check it out. I'd like to stay there at least one night and I quite like the idea of taking a tent and sleeping out in the open air. Are you allowed to camp there?
[05:24] Man: That would be lovely, but I'm afraid...

passages.title: Kenvale School Fair
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Kenvale School Fair"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:38] AUDIO: Good evening and thank you for coming to the Kenvale School Fair Volunteers Meeting. As you know, this is the biggest fundraising event in the school year, and as usual we're expecting lots of people to come, which is why we're starting to prepare now, six months before the big day. I'll begin tonight by talking about the different volunteer roles, so you can decide what you'd like to do. The entertainment coordinator position involves deciding what kinds of rides and activities will be at the fair, and making sure there's a good variety of things to do.

[01:15] AUDIO: From past experience, this role involves a lot of liaising with other helpers and the entertainers, which means that most of the work is done after office hours. We need an advertising and promotion coordinator to make sure that people hear about the fair, and lots of people come. We know this is a big job, so we've decided to have a couple of people doing it to share the load. The parent who did this role last year has just been offered a job, which starts next month, so she won't be able to lend us the benefit of her experience, sadly.

[01:52] AUDIO: The technical coordinator makes sure that there is a suitable stage for the performers, and that there are enough speakers and people can hear them and so on. Now, this may sound like a technical background is required, but it's not, as you don't actually have to set up or fix anything yourself. Having a car is essential, though, because in the week leading up to the event, you'll need to be able to get to the school early in the mornings, and occasionally later at night. We also need a staffing coordinator.

[02:24] AUDIO: This person will be required to look after the many helpers on the day of the fair. This role has just been created based on our experience of last year's event. We found that our volunteers felt a bit overworked, and so we're hoping that this role will make things easier. It will help to reduce stress if you organise the helpers about a month before the fair.

[03:33] AUDIO: Now, moving on to the map of the school fair, I'll point out some of the more important areas that you'll need to know about, so you can help direct the visitors. You can see that we'll be using the large grounds just behind the school, and we'll set up temporary areas and pathways there. The first thing I'll show you are the fairground rights, which are always popular with the children. If you look at the map, you'll see the fair entrance at the bottom.

[04:00] AUDIO: From there, follow the main path in the direction of the river, and it's the third area on the left, the large rectangular area. The entertainment stage is a big feature of the fair, and this is where everyone will be able to see all the performers. To find this, go straight along the main path until you get to the river. Turn right and follow the path to the end, and there it is.

[04:26] AUDIO: There's not much shade here, so we should remind parents to bring hats for their children. If anyone wants a cold drink or a snack, then they'll ask you where the cafe is. Originally, we were going to put it opposite the toilets, but we've decided to put it near the river to take advantage of the views and breezes. You can see it on the map.

[04:47] AUDIO: It's a circular area, surrounded by trees, near the playground. The first aid tent is always an important part of the fair. We wanted to put that in an area that was easily accessible and a bit separated from the other attractions, but near the entrance. If you look at the map, you'll see it's south of the toilets, not far from the school fence line.

[05:12] AUDIO: The market stools are where visitors will be able to pick up a bargain or some homemade produce. Last year, these were located just south of the meeting area, but the stool holders complained that it was too exposed and hot. So, this year, we've moved them to the north of the meeting area. Lots of good shelter provided by the trees here.

[05:33] AUDIO: Of course, there'll be the ever-popular pony rides. To reach these, direct visitors to follow the main path from the entrance until they reach the L-shaped area on the left, next to the playground. Now, as I was saying ...

passages.title: Evaluating Environmental Research Course Modules
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Evaluating Environmental Research Course Modules"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:50] Jamie: Hi Martha, do you have time to talk? We have to submit our evaluations of our course next week and I thought it'd be useful to discuss what we both think.
[01:00] Martha: Good idea, that would help refresh my memory, especially about things we did in previous years.
[01:06] Jamie: I agree, so let's talk about the modules we took. What about statistics for environmental research? I've always been hopeless with numbers so I thought that I'd learn a lot.
[01:18] Martha: But you know, it wasn't at a high enough level for me. I actually had to do a lot of reading on my own.
[01:25] Jamie: Me too, I had to get an additional reading list from the tutor.
[01:29] Martha: Now, sewage and drainage systems, I wasn't looking forward to that one.
[01:35] Jamie: Not exactly a pleasant subject, but you know, the module convinced me that it's an essential topic to understand for both cities and rural environments.
[01:45] Martha: Right, and in the end, not a boring subject.
[01:50] Jamie: Not at all, it was quite a revelation.
[01:53] Martha: The module on agriculture and food security could have been good.
[01:57] Jamie: But the assigned readings were only those ancient government publications.
[02:02] Martha: And the lecture notes clearly hadn't been updated for years.
[02:07] Jamie: I know. What about the module on sustainable energy? I really got into the project we had to do to invent something functional. I devised a windmill to power my laptop.
[02:19] Martha: Yep, the projects were great. So hands-on. Though the personal battery charger I built never really worked.
[02:27] Jamie: Too bad, but I'm sure you learned a lot nonetheless.
[02:31] Martha: I did. And the government policy module? I wish it had included policy in other countries. It was a bit inward-looking, I thought, focused just on this country.
[02:42] Jamie: I mentioned that to the lecturer, but she said it was best to concentrate on one country in depth at first.

[02:49] Martha: Maybe. And there was that module called water management. I must admit, I got lost in the discussion about the issues of groundwater levels and flood risk management, which weren't that essential.
[03:02] Jamie: You weren't the only one.
[03:40] Martha: OK. I thought some aspects of the course organisation were particularly helpful. Can we talk a bit about that?
[03:48] Jamie: Of course.
[03:50] Martha: Actually, I was disappointed that I couldn't take any module whenever I wanted.
[03:55] Jamie: That's true. But the variety of modules on offer was a strong point and meant I managed to cover a lot of subjects.
[04:02] Martha: Me too. More than I expected.
[04:05] Jamie: I had wanted to finish the course early by doing an extra module each term, which would have been useful, but unfortunately that wasn't allowed.
[04:15] Martha: I had to wait to do some modules, which I found hard to schedule. And I think more assigned reading for the modules would have made the lectures easier to follow.
[04:26] Jamie: That would have been good. But I was pleased that the course organizers were able to provide modules focusing on real life issues, which we can apply later when looking for jobs.
[04:36] Martha: True. And I would have hated it if it had all been theory.
[04:40] Jamie: What about the written paper we had to do for Dr. Brown? Are there any things we could suggest to improve the way that's handled?
[04:48] Martha: Well, I got lots of help from Dr. Brown and his assistant in narrowing down what I wanted to write about.
[04:54] Jamie: Yes, they stopped me from doing something too ambitious. But choosing a topic right at the beginning of the module was difficult.
[05:03] Martha: Maybe he could postpone the decision until halfway through the term.
[05:06] Jamie: Good idea. I was happy with the word limit for the assignment though.
[05:10] Martha: Well, as usual, I could have written on and on, but the limit made me refine my thoughts, so it was OK in the end.
[05:19] Jamie: I wish I could have had a session with Dr. Brown after he'd marked my written paper. I know it would be time consuming, but it would have been really useful.
[05:29] Martha: Actually, I was satisfied with Dr. Brown's written feedback. It was amazingly detailed, so I don't think I needed more.
[05:37] Jamie: But I wish they could arrange sessions where students get together and help each other before submitting their written work.
[05:44] Martha: Good idea. If they provided time for that, it would be quite convenient.
[05:49] Jamie: Right. Now that we've almost finished our course, it's time to think about our career prospects. What type of organization do you hope to work for?

passages.title: The Music of Salvatore Sciarrino
content: 📌 The Music of Salvatore Sciarrino

Biographical details
• He was born in Palermo in 1947
• He moved to Rome in 1969 and took a course in electronic music, which influenced his style as a composer.

Work
• In the 1970s he composed a lot of music and taught until 1982.
• As well as music, he has written many [ _____ ].
• He has won many awards – including one in 2011 for [ _____ ] in music.

Musical characteristics
• Surprisingly, his music often features [ _____ ] and very soft sounds.
• His music uses unusual instrument techniques, e.g. violins often produce sounds which resemble those found in [ _____ ].
• He is seen as a [ _____ ] of music.
• Sciarrino compares his music to a distant [ _____ ].

Concert piece
• For piano, chorus and orchestra
• Finished in 1979 and written in memory of a [ _____ ]
• Very difficult to play
• Starts with a noise that sounds like [ _____ ], produced by two people moving large pieces of [ _____ ]
• Although the music is unusual, it has a traditional [ _____ ]
transcript: [01:07] AUDIO: Good morning. We're really pleased that our university is going to hold a concert featuring the music of the Italian composer Salvatore Schiarino. He's considered one of the leading composers of modern classical music in Europe. His music is highly unusual, so in order to prepare you for this concert, I'm going to talk about his life and music.

[01:35] AUDIO: First, some biographical details. Salvatore Schiarino was born in the Italian city of Palermo in 1947. Though he did receive some music lessons, he is mainly self-taught as a composer. After a few years of university in his home city, he moved to Rome in 1969, where he studied electronic music.

[02:04] AUDIO: This experience served as a turning point in the development of Schiarino as a composer. Turning to his work, he composed a great deal in the 1970s and was a music teacher until 1982. Apart from composing music and teaching, he has also produced a large number of essays on a range of topics, such as the philosophy behind his work and musical form. Throughout his career, he has won numerous prestigious awards, most notably a major prize in 2011, which recognized his musical originality.

[02:49] AUDIO: So you could say that he is one of the most important composers of our times. Now I'll talk about the characteristics of his music, which some people are a bit surprised by. The first thing that many listeners will notice about Schiarino's music is the frequent use of silence. What is also striking about his music is his preference for extremely soft sounds that are sometimes at such a low volume that they can hardly be heard.

[03:28] AUDIO: The other unusual aspect of his music is that he frequently requires musicians to play their instruments in unconventional ways, so that, for example, a violin may end up sounding very strange and creating sounds we generally associate with nature. Actually, his novel instrumental techniques have often been imitated by other composers. As a result, he is widely regarded as a pioneer in terms of creating new sounds. It may sound strange, but Schiarino himself has likened his music to a volcano viewed from afar.

[04:13] AUDIO: As you'll see, it builds up slowly to an exciting climax. Let's move on to talk about the particular piece that we'll hear at the concert. Many people consider it to be his finest work to date. It's an immense piece of music for piano, chorus, and orchestra that was completed in 1979.

[04:40] AUDIO: The work is dedicated to a friend who died unexpectedly, so it was written as a kind of memorial. In many ways, it is representative of his work as a whole in terms of the sound that it creates. It's technically formidable, and it's a very challenging piece for musicians to play. The piece opens with a low sound of great complexity that is similar to thunder.

[05:11] AUDIO: This low-pitched noise is sustained almost uninterrupted for 45 minutes, which may sound quite boring, but I found it to be very haunting and atmospheric. The sound, by the way, is created by large vibrating sheets of metal, which are slowly manipulated by two percussionists. There are very quiet and strange chords produced by string instruments and very complex piano melodies that quietly appear and then disappear. Even though the piece will be, for many people, very unusual in terms of the sounds it creates, it actually has a very conventional structure, which is just another surprising aspect of Schiarino's work.
[06:05] AUDIO: Now let's move on to another work...

transcript: [00:08] Daniel: London Relocation Services, Daniel speaking. How may I help you?
[00:14] Anna: Good morning. My family and I are moving to London later this year and I wonder if you can help?
[00:20] Daniel: Sure. First of all, I'll need to get some personal details. May I take your full name, please?
[00:27] Anna: It's Anna Woods.
[00:29] Daniel: Thanks. Where are you moving from?
[00:32] Anna: Northern Ireland, just outside Belfast, actually.
[00:36] Daniel: Right. And what's your current address?
[00:39] Anna: It's 118 Fordyce Park. I'll spell that for you. It's F-O-R-D-Y-C-E and that's in Ballysilham.
[00:53] Daniel: And what's the postcode?
[01:00] Daniel: All right. And could I take a contact phone number?
[01:05] Anna: I'll give you my mobile number as you can get me on that anytime. It's 078400-51963.
[01:17] Daniel: Great. Got that. Now, we always like to get a bit more information about the families that we're moving. It helps with the search.
[01:26] Daniel: Are you moving for work?
[01:28] Anna: Yes, my husband's just got a new job in London.
[01:31] Daniel: And what about you? Do you work?
[01:34] Anna: Well, I've been working as a teaching assistant recently, but I'm actually a qualified nurse and I'd like to get back into that if possible.
[01:43] Daniel: Right. And do you have any children?
[01:46] Anna: Yes, a son. So we need to find a school for him.
[01:50] Daniel: Is it a secondary school you'll be looking for?
[01:53] Anna: No, he's still in primary school. He's not quite at the secondary level yet.
[01:58] Daniel: Fine. So let's go on to talk about your requirements for the property. Do you have a preferred location? Is your husband's job in the centre?
[02:08] Anna: No, it's in East London, but we'd rather live somewhere quieter.
[02:13] Daniel: Sure. There are some lovely areas in the south.
[02:16] Anna: OK, that sounds great. Now, my husband doesn't want to spend too long commuting to work every day.
[02:23] Daniel: So I imagine that ideally he'd like to be not too far from a station then?
[02:30] Anna: Yes, he drives now, but I guess that's not going to be possible and he's not keen on buses.
[02:36] Daniel: What about you or your son? Do you have any preferences? Does your son do any sport, for example?
[02:43] Anna: He's quite active, so I'm sure he'd love a park nearby to run around in. He doesn't do swimming or anything like that.
[02:51] Daniel: Great. So what sort of property do you have in mind?
[03:30] Anna: We have friends who live in an amazing flat over there, but as we've always lived in a house, I think we'll stick with that. We'd find it hard to adapt to a flat.
[03:40] Daniel: OK. And size-wise, how many bedrooms would you like?
[03:45] Anna: Well, there's just myself, my husband and our son.
[03:49] Daniel: So you definitely need a two-bedroom property. But how about having a guest room? I might be able to find a three-bedroom property for you.
[03:58] Anna: Yes, that would be ideal. We're sure to have family visiting often.
[04:03] Daniel: Alright, I've made a note of that. Now, are there any other requirements for your new property?
[04:09] Anna: Hmm. Well, it's not essential, but it'd be handy to have an office for when my husband works from home. It doesn't need to be a big one.
[04:19] Anna: I guess it all comes down to budget.
[04:22] Daniel: Yes. OK, Anna. Well, I've certainly got enough to be getting on with and I...

passages.title: Starting work at Hollies supermarket
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Starting work at Hollies supermarket"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:54] AUDIO: Welcome to Holly's Supermarket. I'm sure you'll all enjoy working in our dedicated team here. So, what will you be doing? Well, we're open Monday through Sunday, so you'll need to be able to work weekends as well as irregular weekday shifts.

[01:12] AUDIO: These sometimes start at 5am or finish at 11pm. Your duties will include checking and unpacking lorry deliveries, as well as working on the shop floor, stocking shelves and so on. But you'll only be required to do manual lifting if the goods are light. When the store is very busy, you'll also have to assess changing priorities.

[01:39] AUDIO: For example, if there's a queue at the tills, you'll jump on a spare one to help. If you notice something's been spilt and the surface is a little bit wet, you'll get a mop to clean it up. No need to check with the manager first. Similarly, if bakery items are selling quickly, you'll help cook some more.

[01:59] AUDIO: And if a customer can't find, say, the apples, you'll instantly leave what you're doing and show them. But you'll still get time off to relax too, of course. We pride ourselves on a positive attitude here. A little small talk shows you're interested in customers and are providing excellent service, just as long as you don't overdo it and keep another customer waiting.

[02:25] AUDIO: And always smile. It forces you to stay positive and being generally upbeat makes your whole team happy too. This increases efficiency and gives a good impression to customers. If it's quiet, help someone pack their bags.

[02:42] AUDIO: Customers really appreciate it, especially when they've bought more than they expected to. Staying calm's also a necessity. passages.title: Picture Books' Use in Early Childhood Education
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Picture Books' Use in Early Childhood Education"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:52] Girl: Hi, are you ready to discuss our presentation?
[00:55] Boy: Yeah, sure.
[00:56] Girl: So, what are we going to say about teachers reading picture books with young children?
[01:01] Boy: I think we should start with the reasons why teachers use picture books.
[01:05] Girl: The journal article we read mentioned several picture books and why they're popular with teachers.
[01:11] Boy: Right, like I Spy Friends. It's a lovely story.
[01:14] Girl: Yeah, the children like to find the familiar faces from the fairy tales they know so well.
[01:20] Boy: And they're all doing predictable things. The article said children find this familiarity very comforting.
[01:26] Girl: Yes. Now, how about Goodnight Little Rabbit, which has those delightful pictures. I love the way the colours get darker as the book progresses, indicating how evening turns into night.
[01:39] Boy: Me too. The article said that's why teachers like it.
[01:42] Girl: Very cute. And a good example of visual subtext. Hard to believe that it came out over 60 years ago. It's still relevant.
[01:51] Boy: I really liked what the article said about the boat party. There's a lot of repetition, which I think would be great for vocabulary development.
[01:59] Girl: That's true. But apparently it's the images that make it popular with children. The artist is really well known and children often ask for her books.
[02:08] Boy: Oh, that's good to know.
[02:10] Girl: And shall we also include Puppy and Friends?

[02:13] Boy: Yes. It sounds like an innocent title, but the article warns that there's a bit of a fright, you know, the one on the last page when the puppy suddenly encounters the scary cat. Teachers like to use this to help children explore their emotions.
[02:26] Girl: Sounds good. Hats and Socks is a good one. It doesn't really have a beginning and an end, does it? Which is unusual.
[02:35] Boy: That's why teachers like this one though. Because it's so different, it's good for children to hear a story that doesn't follow the usual pattern.
[02:43] Girl: And the pages are so full of life and colour. A good choice.
[02:47] Boy: Hmm.

[02:48] Girl: Okay. And for our last one, how about A Family Adventure? This one uses a lot of the same language throughout, which I think can help with letter and word recognition. Teachers say it has a really poetic feel to it.
[03:04] Girl: They often sing it to a simple tune.
[03:06] Boy: Yes. And it's full of beautiful watercolors too.

[03:45] Girl: In the next part of our presentation, shall we look at some of the other research? I really liked Smith's article about the history of picture books. Picture books haven't been around for that long, of course. And as we know from our reading lists, there's a lot of research on them already.
[04:02] Girl: Smith makes some interesting points.
[04:04] Boy: Yes. One thing that shocked me was that some people don't consider picture books as proper writing because they don't have enough words in them.

[04:12] Girl: Yes, that was unexpected for me as well. I think they should be just as respected as other works of fiction. Smith also mentioned that books from other countries are very popular here, even though they don't show our daily life. I think that's interesting.
[04:27] Boy: But it's the same for adult fiction too. People want variety. What I didn't realise is how fixed the number of pages is.
[04:35] Girl: Me neither. I wasn't expecting that they're so strictly limited to 32 pages. It's important, so let's include it.
[04:44] Boy: All right. Now let's think about other aspects of picture books we want to include in our presentation. How about the characters?

[04:52] Girl: Okay, well, a lot of them feature animals or families often in very traditional roles. But do you think we need to talk about that? For me, the main thing is that they are mostly printed as board books. The cardboard material makes it easy for young children to turn their pages.
[05:10] Boy: I agree. And it's essential for children to hold books and learn how they open at the front and that the text goes in a certain direction.
[05:17] Girl: Good point. Why don't we also discuss how culture is important in picture books, like the importance of respecting the elderly?
[05:26] Boy: Yes, it's probably different all over the world. Would it be interesting to make a comparison between modern and historical picture books and consider future directions for the genre?
[05:36] Girl: It sounds interesting, but I don't have any research on that, so we'd better leave it.
[05:42] Boy: So, what's next? We don't need…

passages.title: Geography – 331 Field Trip
content: 📌 Geography – 331 Field Trip

The James Bay Road
At the starting point of the road, everyone must stop for [ _____ ].
For safety reasons, there are [ _____ ] on the highway.

Radisson Research Centre
The Centre works with other institutes to research the region's [ _____ ].
Security is the responsibility of Hydro Quebec.
Lectures will discuss the effect of [ _____ ] on the land.
Outpost stations gather and publish research related to variations in the [ _____ ].

The Trans-Taiga Road
The road is unpaved.
Breakdowns are serious as car [ _____ ] are expensive.
At hydro stations, engineers will discuss hydro production and the impact of rainfall.

The Taiga
There are not many types of [ _____ ], but a good range of wildlife.
The area known as Muskeg is dangerous as it has hidden [ _____ ].
Photographs of birds should be taken for future [ _____ ].
Water samples will be checked for [ _____ ].
transcript: [01:23] AUDIO: Good morning. Next week is the Geography 331 field trip to the far north of Quebec. Today I'll discuss your trip and your tasks. As you know, you will be close to the Arctic Circle.

[01:39] AUDIO: You're going to travel up the James Bay Road through a region that is very remote and uninhabited, yet very beautiful. The highway is 620 kilometers long, but it's fully paved for the entire length. Where the highway begins, there is a roadside office where you must stop. The road is remote, so your registration is very important in case of an emergency.

[02:09] AUDIO: The office is staffed 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. You have to sign in to go up the road and sign out upon your return. For additional safety, at different places along the highway, telephones have been installed which connect with staff in the office. Remember, there is no mobile service in this remote area.

[02:36] AUDIO: The first work of your field trip is at the end of the James Bay Road in Radisson, a small town of only 300 inhabitants. You will stay at Radisson Research Centre, which works with various universities and Hydro-Québec to carry out studies into the ecology of the region. Because the research centre and the road exist as a result of the development of hydroelectricity complexes in northern Québec, Hydro-Québec is responsible for all emergency assistance and security of all visitors. Your first few days at the centre will be spent attending lectures about their past research.

[03:21] AUDIO: You will hear that they have paid particular attention to any disturbance to the land caused by insects. After that, you will visit the various outpost stations. There are three of them, and when you visit them, you will be able to observe how data on the varying patterns of the climate is collected and published for scientific research. The second part of your field trip is back down the James Bay Road to the Trans-Taga Road, which is the northernmost continuous unpaved road in eastern North America.

[04:03] AUDIO: In fact, it's very uneven gravel, so drivers have to be very careful. Hydro-Québec cautions that driving over rocks on the rough road may cause severe damage to the car. Any breakdown is serious, as repairs are costly. Along the way, you will be stopping at two hydroelectric generating stations, each on a different river.

[04:29] AUDIO: There, you will meet with engineers who will explain and demonstrate how rainfall has an impact on producing electric energy. Your last two days of the trip will be spent camping out in the taiga on the Canadian Shield. Taiga is the Russian term for a type of forest. You will find the region is relatively poor in the number of plant species, yet there is a great variety of wildlife that can be seen.

[05:00] AUDIO: You'll go to an area that once had forest fires, and you'll see how the landscape has naturally small rocky hills which confine the lower wetlands. These low-lying areas are called muskeg, which is made up of slowly decomposing plants. It is not safe to walk on it, as it has pools that are not easily seen, so keep to the rocks. The muskeg is home to many small birds and waterfowl.

[05:31] AUDIO: In fact, there are at least 60 varieties, so keep your waterproof digital cameras handy so you can take plenty of pictures. Then we will have documentation of the existing waterfowl, as some are becoming extinct. Water is a problem in this area, so you'll also be collecting test tubes of water to bring back to our research lab for analysis. It needs to be monitored for pollution that may be caused by rainfall coming from the south.
